name: Grecian Formula

card.summary: A men's progressive hair color liquid used daily in place of shampoo-style routines to gradually darken gray hair for a natural, younger-looking blend.
card.note: Earlier formulas used lead acetate, which regulators later removed from hair dyes; current versions use other ingredients.

quick.overview:
Grecian Formula is a long-running brand of progressive hair color made by Combe, aimed mainly at men. Instead of an all-at-once dye job, it darkens gray or white hair gradually over repeated applications, so the change looks natural rather than abrupt.

The appeal is a subtle, discreet way to look younger by softening gray at the temples and through the hair, without the obvious jump of a salon color.
quick.how: Users apply the liquid or foam to dry or damp hair on a repeated schedule until the preferred shade is reached, then continue periodically to maintain it. Results build over days to weeks, and the label directions control how often to apply. Combe markets related products such as Just For Men.
quick.risks: Earlier versions relied on lead acetate, which regulators moved to bar from hair dyes; consumer groups filed complaints from 2018, and bismuth citrate is cited as the replacement. As with any hair color, a patch test for allergy is the usual labeled precaution.

lead: Grecian Formula is a brand of progressive hair coloring made by Combe Incorporated, a personal care company founded in 1949 and based in White Plains, New York.[1][2] It is designed to darken gray hair gradually over repeated applications, giving a natural-looking blend that men use to look younger without a dramatic change.[1]

Historically the colorant was lead acetate, which reacts with sulfur in hair keratin to form dark lead sulfide inside the shaft, building color over time.[1] Wikipedia describes lead acetate as the former active ingredient in gradual darkening products such as Grecian Formula.[3] After complaints from consumer and environmental groups in 2018 and regulatory action on lead acetate, the brand moved to bismuth citrate, according to Combe's Wikipedia page.[2]
Combe also sells Just for Men, introduced in 1987.[2] Sources date the end of lead acetate in hair dye differently, and no clinical trials of the brand have been published.

chain: Repeated application deposits color in gray hair
Hair looks younger and more even
angle.text: Users apply it repeatedly so gray darkens a little at a time, avoiding the sharp contrast of a one-time dye. It is aimed at men who want subtle gray reduction.

paras: Progressive colorants build color rather than coating hair at once. In the lead-acetate formulation, the metal salt penetrated the cuticle and reacted with sulfur in keratin to form dark nanoparticles inside the shaft, with color becoming noticeable after weeks of repeated use.[1] Gray coverage in general typically needs touch-ups every few weeks as new roots grow in.[3]

Grokipedia reports the brand launching in the early 1960s and attributes its formula to a lead-acetate compound that its sources link to a wartime observation in Greece; this account has not been independently confirmed.[1] Combe has owned the brand throughout.[1][2]

In 2018 the Environmental Defense Fund and other groups filed a complaint with the FDA seeking removal of lead acetate from Grecian Formula and other hair dyes.[2] Combe's page states lead acetate has been banned since January 2022 and bismuth citrate replaced it, while Grokipedia gives a 2018 date for the reformulation.[1][2]

timeline.event: Consumer and environmental groups file FDA complaint about lead acetate in hair dyes.[2]
